domain: Safety Engineering / Organizational Learning / High-Reliability Systems
topic_summary: Analysis of how aviation and nuclear industries retain catastrophe-avoidance competence across decades without recurring disasters. The kernel contest centers on whether simulation exercises constitute genuine practice of safety-critical skills or whether only actual catastrophic events provide the selection pressure necessary to maintain competence.

key_entities: Aviation stall recovery protocols (FAA-mandated simulator training for loss-of-control scenarios)
Nuclear reactor operators (emergency response drills, control room simulators)
Actual catastrophic events (Three Mile Island, Tenerife, AF447)
Regulatory bodies (FAA, NRC; mandate simulation frequency and fidelity)
key_tensions: Simulation fidelity vs real-world unpredictability (can drills capture chaos?)
Competence decay vs catastrophe frequency (decades between events; how is skill retained?)
key_mechanisms: Simulator-based skill maintenance (scheduled drills as substitute for real events)
Incident learning propagation (near-misses and foreign accidents analyzed industry-wide)
Regulatory enforcement of training cycles (FAA Part 121 recurrent training; NRC operator licensing)
key_absences: Medical crisis management (lacks high-fidelity simulation infrastructure; sepsis/cardiac arrest competence retention unclear)
Decay measurement (no quantitative metric for how fast catastrophe-avoidance skills atrophy without practice)

commitment_system_recognition.kernel_description: The shared commitment that catastrophe-avoidance competence must be maintained across long periods without actual catastrophes
commitment_system_recognition.authority_description: Regulatory bodies (FAA, NRC) mandate training cycles; professional norms define acceptable practice

readings.commitment: High-fidelity simulation constitutes genuine practice; drills are functionally equivalent to real catastrophic events for competence maintenance
readings.expected_structural_delta: Simulation infrastructure becomes critical; competence decay manageable via scheduled drills; regulatory enforcement sufficient

readings.commitment: Only actual catastrophes provide the selection pressure (chaos, mortality salience, organizational trauma) necessary to maintain competence
readings.expected_structural_delta: Long peacetime periods = inevitable competence decay; simulation creates false confidence; industry vulnerable to black swan re-emergence

readings.commitment: Neither simulation alone nor catastrophe alone sufficient; competence maintained via distributed learning from near-misses, foreign incidents, and high-realism drills
readings.expected_structural_delta: Competence retention depends on incident-sharing networks; industries with strong cross-organizational learning (aviation) succeed; those without (medicine?) fail

axiom_contradictions.basis: One holds that drills replicate the critical selection mechanism; the other holds that only real catastrophes provide mortality salience and organizational trauma necessary for competence retention. No framework can hold both the sufficiency of simulation AND the necessity of actual catastrophe simultaneously.

omegas.description: Medicine lacks high-fidelity simulation infrastructure for crisis scenarios (sepsis, code blue). Does competence retention fail there, or is distributed real-event frequency (every hospital has codes) sufficient? Tests necessity of either simulation OR catastrophe centrality.

How fast do catastrophe-avoidance skills decay without practice? No quantitative industry metric. If decay is slow (years), simulation_as_proxy_catastrophe is stronger. If fast (months), catastrophe_as_necessary_selector gains support.

Does the D5 break (drills-as-proxy-catastrophe collapse) occur? If simulation and catastrophe are structurally identical for competence maintenance, the kernel contest dissolves. If they differ in mortality salience or chaos fidelity, readings remain distinct.
omegas.source: User's kernel contest flag + axiom contradiction test

omegas.description: Aviation shows decades-long competence retention; nuclear similar. Do industries WITHOUT strong simulation infrastructure (e.g., dam failure management, pandemic response) show faster decay? If yes, supports simulation_as_proxy_catastrophe. If no, supports catastrophe_as_necessary_selector or hybrid_near_miss_learning.
omegas.source: Dark Matter Probe 2 (absence of non-aviation/nuclear comparisons in extraction)

fracture_scan.notes: No fractures detected. Kernel decomposition produces three structurally distinct readings with measurable structural deltas. Axiom contradiction declared between simulation_as_proxy_catastrophe and catastrophe_as_necessary_selector (sufficiency of drills vs necessity of real chaos). Hybrid_near_miss_learning occupies intermediate position with distinct observable (incident-sharing network density).
